question: Can a woman uncover her hair in front of a man who has come to propose to her?
asked: In a recent lecture I mentioned in passing that a lady may show her hair to a man who is interested in proposing to her, and I received at least a dozen comments, emails and tweets from people who were confused and wanted to verify whether I actually said this. So the question is: what may a lady show to a man who comes to propose to her? Before the nikah, and in the presence of her mahrams, may she uncover her hair and show herself without her hijab, or must she wear the hijab?
answer:
The majority position on this issue is that the one who proposes, the man who comes to propose for a lady's hand or who is interested in a lady's hand, does not occupy any different status than any other non-relative, any other non-mahram. And hence three of the four schools, the Shafi'is, the Malikis and the Hanafis, say: under no circumstance. I think there's one position in the Malikis, or the Shafi'is, but generally speaking, the default of these three madhhabs is that for a lady who is interested in a man, and a man interested in a lady, before the nikah nothing changes. And therefore she is not allowed to take off her hijab.

We're obviously talking about a situation where there is no privacy; they're not alone. They are sitting, let's say, in her parents' house and he comes to propose, or he comes to talk to her in a public place.

And of course, by unanimous consensus really, or we should say all of the schools say, that the husband-to-be and the wife-to-be should visit or see one another in the presence of their mahrams. This is something that is encouraged by all the scholars. The other cultural habit, of not knowing your wife at all, not even knowing what she looks like until the marriage night, is something that is gone; nobody does that anymore. But there were cultural limitations back in the day, and it was not uncommon for a person to get married without even knowing how the spouse looks. The Sunnah came and encouraged that the spouses should see one another and make sure that there is compatibility, because this is a lifelong commitment. So there's no major controversy over this.

The issue is whether she may take her hijab off or not. As I said, the default position of the Shafi'is, the Malikis and the Hanafis is that no, she should not and she may not; she is not allowed to do that.

In the Hanbali school, the mashhur or well-known position, which Imam Ahmad also explicitly said, is that she may actually take off her hijab if she chooses to do so. There must be a mahram present: her father, her brother, her other relatives are there. She may appear in front of the man interested in her the way that she appears in front of her own mahrams. So how she dresses in front of her father, in front of her brother: in other words, she's dressing in basically normal clothes, but maybe her hair is uncovered, maybe the full jilbab is not on her. She's wearing, let's say, a loose blouse and a loose skirt, or a loose shirt and loose pants. How she would appear in front of her own mahrams, Imam Ahmad basically said it is allowed for her to appear in such a manner in front of the fiancé-to-be. Allowed, not required, not necessary. She cannot be forced; it's her choice, her prerogative, if she wants to do so.

And they base this on a number of evidences, primarily two. The first of them is the hadith in Abu Dawud and Muslim, Imam Ahmad and others, narrated by Jabir ibn Abdullah radiyAllahu ta'ala 'anhu, that the Prophet ﷺ said: if one of you proposes to a lady, "if he can see that which will make him want to propose for her, then let him do that."

So Jabir radiyAllahu ta'ala 'anhu said that he proposed to a lady from the Ansar, and he would look at her. Now, this sounds very scary and very freaky when you translate it, but it translates as: "I would hide and look at her without her knowledge, until finally I saw her and I wanted to propose, and I proposed and ended up marrying her." What this means is not that he would, a'udhu billah, spy inside her house. What it means is that he would wait outside the house, and when she would come out she would not know that there's a man who is basically interested in her, so he would look at her. And obviously in our times this is raising alarm bells, spying and whatnot.

So the point is that the Hanabilah, the Hanbali scholars, have taken this incident and said that it is allowed to look at her the way that she would normally be. So for example, if she were to just come out of her house and, let's say, I don't know, feed the chickens, whatever it might be, or hang the laundry, she's not dressed in the full jilbab or whatnot. And Jabir radiyAllahu 'anhu was basically looking at her the way that she might appear in front of her parents.

And there's also an incident of Umar ibn al-Khattab radiyAllahu 'anhu, in which he proposed to the daughter of Ali ibn Abi Talib radiyAllahu 'anhu, and he also looked at more than just the jilbab and whatnot. So they interpret this: he looked at that which might not normally be apparent when she goes outside, and which might be apparent only in front of the mahrams. So this incident is then taken as evidence, the fact that Umar ibn al-Khattab did this and Ali approved, or he knew that this was happening. And so they know that this is something allowed for them to do.

So based on these and other evidences, the well-known position of the Hanbali school is that when the man comes to propose, or he's interested in proposing, the lady may choose to opt for this. Again, it's not mandatory; she doesn't have to do this. She may appear in front of him the way that she appears in front of her father and her brother, however she dresses normally. So that is a decent covering: most of her body is covered, it's loose clothing obviously, because in our Shariah it is not allowed for a lady to appear in front of her mahrams in suggestive clothing, in extremely tight or skimpy garments. This is not allowed. She has to dress with some dignity in front of her father and brothers. And that same level she may display, if she wants to, in front of somebody who wants to marry her, if she wants him to marry her.

In fact, some of my own teachers, and I remember this clearly, this went back and forth on this issue: some of our students wanted to confirm, and they heard this from our Shaykh, that he literally said she is allowed to even beautify herself in the way that would be acceptable and normal. In other words, not in an extremely vulgar manner, but just the basic makeup and whatnot. If she wished to do so, she may do so. In other words, if she wishes to show herself to be who she is, regularly speaking, with a little bit of makeup and her hair and whatnot, this is allowed for her if she wants to do so.

Now again, this is the minority opinion. It is the Hanbali position, or one of the positions of the Hanbali school; the other three generally do not allow this. Nonetheless, the texts of the hadith and also the incidents, and there are a number of incidents in the lives of the Sahabah, indicate that this was understood and known to them. And that's why I said it in passing without going into all these details. **But now that people ask, this is the position that I hold.** It is the fatwa given in most Hanbali schools to this day, by scholars of this day as well. And there are evidences in the Qur'an and the Sunnah in this regard. Nonetheless, if somebody chooses to follow the majority position, that is their prerogative. And Allah knows best.
